title: Job 15:1–16
context: Eliphaz the Temanite begins the second round of speeches with a sharper tone than in chapters 4–5. He accuses Job of empty words, of undermining the fear of God, and of presuming to wisdom beyond the aged. He repeats his earlier claim (4:17-19) that no human is clean before God. Some of what he says is true in general, but he applies it to Job as an accusation, and the book later records God’s verdict that the friends did not speak rightly of him (42:7).

verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz the Temanite answers Job a second time. Arminian readers note that the speaker is one of the friends whose words God will later rebuke, so his claims must be weighed carefully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Eliphaz opens the second round of speeches. Like his first speech, this one mixes recognizable truths with a mistaken application to Job’s situation.

verses.text: “Should a wise man answer with vain knowledge, and fill himself with the east wind?
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz asks whether a wise man should answer with vain knowledge and fill himself with the east wind. Arminian readers see him dismissing Job’s words as empty and hot air.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the east wind, a scorching desert wind, suggests words that are harsh and useless. Eliphaz is no longer gentle; he openly mocks Job’s speeches.

verses.text: Should he reason with unprofitable talk, or with speeches with which he can do no good?
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz asks whether Job should argue with unprofitable talk. Arminian readers see the friend refusing to hear the substance of Job’s complaint, treating it only as useless speech.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Eliphaz judges Job’s words by their usefulness rather than their honesty. His impatience shows that the friends are no longer listening.

verses.text: Yes, you do away with fear, and hinder devotion before God.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz charges Job with doing away with fear and hindering devotion before God. Arminian readers note the irony: the narrator introduced Job as one who feared God (1:1).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Eliphaz accusing Job of undermining piety itself. The reader knows from chapters 1–2 that this charge is unfounded, which colors everything Eliphaz says.

verses.text: For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the language of the crafty.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says Job’s iniquity teaches his mouth and that he chooses crafty language. Arminian readers see the friend reading guilt into Job’s words rather than hearing his pain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Eliphaz assumes Job’s suffering proves hidden sin, and now treats his protests as further proof. The argument has become circular and closed to correction.

verses.text: Your own mouth condemns you, and not I. Yes, your own lips testify against you.
verses.arminianNotes: Your own mouth condemns you, and not I. Arminian readers see Eliphaz trying to make Job’s words the evidence against him, shifting responsibility away from his own accusation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Eliphaz uses Job’s honest lament as proof of guilt. The book will later vindicate Job’s speech over that of his friends (42:7).

verses.text: “Are you the first man who was born? Or were you brought out before the hills?
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz asks whether Job was the first man born, or brought forth before the hills. Arminian readers see sarcasm aimed at what Eliphaz takes to be Job’s claim to special wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase before the hills resembles the description of wisdom in Proverbs 8:25. Eliphaz mocks Job as if he claimed to be wisdom itself.

verses.text: Have you heard the secret counsel of God? Do you limit wisdom to yourself?
verses.arminianNotes: Have you heard the secret counsel of God? Do you limit wisdom to yourself? Arminian readers note the irony that Eliphaz himself claims special insight while denying it to Job.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the reader has seen something of God’s counsel in chapters 1–2, which neither Job nor Eliphaz knows. Eliphaz’s question cuts against his own certainty.

verses.text: What do you know that we don’t know? What do you understand which is not in us?
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz asks what Job knows that the friends do not. Arminian readers see a refusal to consider that suffering might teach something the comfortable have not learned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Eliphaz claims equal or greater understanding. The book shows that none of the human speakers understands the full situation behind Job’s suffering.

verses.text: With us are both the gray-headed and the very aged men, much older than your father.
verses.arminianNotes: With us are both the gray-headed and the very aged men, much older than your father. Arminian readers see an appeal to age and tradition as a substitute for engaging Job’s actual argument.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that age and tradition are respected in wisdom literature, yet Elihu will later observe that age alone does not guarantee understanding (32:9).

verses.text: Are the consolations of God too small for you, even the word that is gentle toward you?
verses.arminianNotes: Are the consolations of God too small for you, even the word that is gentle toward you? Arminian readers see Eliphaz presenting his own speeches as God’s comfort, which Job has not found comforting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Eliphaz equates his counsel with divine consolation. His words were not as gentle as he claims, and the book does not accept his self-assessment.

verses.text: Why does your heart carry you away? Why do your eyes flash,
verses.arminianNotes: Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash? Arminian readers see Eliphaz reading Job’s emotion as rebellion rather than as the grief of a suffering man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Eliphaz focuses on Job’s demeanor. He treats intensity of feeling as evidence of a heart turned away from God, not of deep grief.

verses.text: that you turn your spirit against God, and let such words go out of your mouth?
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz charges Job with turning his spirit against God. Arminian readers note that Job’s complaints are directed to God, which shows engagement rather than abandonment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Eliphaz cannot distinguish between honest lament and rebellion. The lament psalms show that faithful people may speak boldly to God in distress.

verses.text: What is man, that he should be clean? What is he who is born of a woman, that he should be righteous?
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz asks what man is, that he should be clean or righteous. Arminian readers grant that no human is sinless before God, a truth stated elsewhere in Scripture (Psalm 143:2), while noting that Eliphaz uses it to accuse Job.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the statement is true as far as it goes and relates to the universal reach of sin discussed in the Romans 5:12 box. Eliphaz misapplies it to Job, whom God called blameless (1:8).

verses.text: Behold, he puts no trust in his holy ones. Yes, the heavens are not clean in his sight;
verses.arminianNotes: God puts no trust in his holy ones, and the heavens are not clean in his sight. Arminian readers note that Eliphaz repeats his earlier argument from 4:18 in closely similar words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the contrast between God’s holiness and created beings is real. Eliphaz’s error is not in affirming God’s holiness but in using it to condemn Job.

verses.text: how much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks iniquity like water!
verses.arminianNotes: How much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks iniquity like water! Arminian readers see Eliphaz moving from a general truth to a harsh description that seems aimed at Job.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the language echoes 4:19 and intensifies it. As a statement about fallen humanity it has truth, but as a verdict on Job it contradicts the narrator’s account.
